note: Quick practice: about five minutes, no long text, and the site can mark every question. Each mission practises one skill.

questions.prompt: A wildlife park is writing to its visitors. Is each sentence formal or informal?

items.label: We regret that the Panda House will be closed on Monday.
Sorry, no pandas on Monday!
Please contact the ticket office if you require a refund.
Give us a shout if you want your money back.
Can't wait to see you all at the weekend.

questions.why: Formal writing uses full sentences and words such as "regret" and "require". Informal writing sounds like talking: short forms such as "can't", and phrases such as "give us a shout".

questions.prompt: You are writing a letter to the park manager to ask about a job. Which opening fits best?
options: Dear Ms Nair, I am writing to ask about work at the park.
To whoever, I want a job with the pandas.
questions.why: A letter about a job is formal. It uses the manager's title and name, and says clearly why you are writing.

questions.prompt: This sentence is from a formal report. One word is too informal.
questions.why: "Awesome" is a word for chatting with friends. A report uses a plain, exact word such as "suitable" or "useful".

questions.prompt: Finish this formal email to the park. Choose the word that fits each gap.
questions.passage: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to {{1}} about the opening times. I would be {{2}} if you could send me a timetable. Yours {{3}}, Sam Field
questions.why: "Enquire" and "grateful" are polite, formal words. A letter that starts "Dear Sir or Madam" ends "Yours faithfully".

questions.prompt: Who would you write to in each way?

items.label: A complaint to the park about a cancelled visit
A message to your cousin about the baby panda
An application to be a volunteer
A post in your family group chat

questions.why: You write formally to people you do not know, or when something is official, such as a complaint or an application. You write informally to family and friends.

questions.prompt: These instructions for buying a ticket from a machine are mixed up. Put them in order.
items: First, touch the screen to start.
Next, choose where you are going.
Then choose a single or a return ticket.
After that, pay with a card or coins.
Finally, take your ticket and your change.
questions.why: The words "first", "next", "then", "after that" and "finally" show the order. You also have to choose a ticket before you can pay for it.

questions.prompt: Choose the word that fits each gap in these directions.
questions.passage: {{1}} you leave the station, turn left. {{2}} walk to the traffic lights. {{3}}, cross the road to the bus stop.
questions.why: "When", "then" and "finally" put the directions in order. "Because" gives a reason and "but" shows a difference, so they do not fit.

questions.prompt: Put this account of a late journey in the order it happened.
items: I reached the bus stop at eight o'clock.
A sign said the 14 bus was running twenty minutes late.
While I waited, I sent a message to my manager.
The bus arrived at twenty past eight.
I got to work just as the shop opened.
questions.why: The times help: eight o'clock comes before twenty past eight. You can only wait after you know the bus is late, and you arrive at work last.

questions.prompt: Which sentence tells you what to do if the machine does not give you a ticket?
sentences: The machine takes cards and coins, but not notes.
Tickets are cheaper after half past nine.
If no ticket is printed, press the green Help button and wait for a member of staff.
Keep your ticket until the end of your journey.
questions.why: Only this sentence says what to do when something goes wrong: press Help and wait for staff.

questions.prompt: These paragraphs from a letter of complaint are mixed up. Put them in order.
items: I am writing to complain about the 14 bus service on Monday 3 March.
The 08:10 bus did not arrive, and there was no notice at the stop.
As a result, I was forty minutes late for work.
I would like to know why the bus was cancelled and what you will do to stop this happening again.
I look forward to your reply.
questions.why: A complaint says why you are writing, then what happened, then how it affected you, then what you want done. The closing line comes last.

questions.prompt: One word in this sentence has a mistake.
questions.why: The shop belongs to the village, so it needs an apostrophe and s: "the village's only shop".

questions.prompt: One word in this sentence is the wrong one.
questions.why: "Their" means belonging to them: their jobs. "There" is for a place.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation mark should end each sentence?

items.label: How far is the nearest station
The bus runs every two hours
What a view
Is there a doctor in the village
Most houses here were built before 1950

questions.why: A question ends with a question mark. A statement ends with a full stop. A short burst of feeling, such as "What a view", ends with an exclamation mark.

questions.prompt: Choose the right word for each gap.
questions.passage: The town has grown {{1}} big for its roads. {{2}} are plans for a new bypass, and residents can give {{3}} views at the library.
questions.why: "Too" means more than is wanted. "There are" starts a statement that something exists. "Their" shows the views belong to the residents.

questions.prompt: One word in this sentence has a mistake.
questions.why: "Its" with no apostrophe means belonging to it: its new plan. "It's" is short for "it is" or "it has".

questions.prompt: What is each piece of writing mainly for?

items.label: Book today and save 20 per cent on your desert tour!
Fill your water bottle before you leave the guesthouse.
The Dead Sea is the lowest place on land.
You will not find a better guide anywhere.
The market opens at eight and closes at four.

questions.why: Writing that informs gives facts. Writing that persuades tries to make you do or believe something. Writing that instructs tells you what to do, often starting with a verb such as "fill".

questions.prompt: Is each sentence a fact or an opinion?

items.label: The walk to the viewpoint takes about two hours.
Sunrise is the best time to visit.
The guesthouse has twelve rooms.
The local bread is delicious.

questions.why: A fact can be checked, such as a time or a number. An opinion is what someone thinks, and words such as "best" and "delicious" are clues.

questions.prompt: A tour company wants you to book. Which sentence is trying to persuade you?
sentences: Do not miss this once-in-a-lifetime trip.
Breakfast is served from seven o'clock.
questions.why: "Do not miss" and "once-in-a-lifetime" are there to make you want to book. The other sentences only give information.

questions.prompt: A leaflet lists what to pack as bullet points. Why are bullet points used?
options: To make each item quick to find
To show which item matters most
questions.why: Bullet points set items out one under another, so a reader can find each one at a glance.

questions.prompt: Which kind of text would you expect each sentence to come from?

items.label: We stayed three nights and would happily go back.
Press and hold the button until the light turns green.
Hurry: only six places left for April!
The guide was friendly, but the minibus was cramped.

questions.why: A review tells you what someone thought after trying something. Instructions tell you what to do. An advert pushes you to buy or book.
